                                         SoPE: Spherical Coordinate-Based Positional Embedding for Enhancing Spatial
                                                                  Perception of 3D LVLMs

                                             Guanting Ye1    Qiyan Zhao3 Wenhao Yu2 Liangyu Yuan4 Mingkai Li5 Xiaofeng Zhang3
                                                             Jianmin Ji2 Yanyong Zhang2 Qing Jiang4 Ka-Veng Yuen 1

                                                                             Corresponding author:             kvyuen@um.edu.mo



                                                                Abstract

                                         3D Large Vision-Language Models (3D LVLMs) built upon
                                         Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable
                                         progress across various multimodal tasks. However, their
                                         inherited position-dependent modeling mechanism, Rotary
                                         Position Embedding (RoPE), remains suboptimal for 3D
                                         multimodal understanding. The vanilla RoPE formula-
                                         tion fails to preserve essential three-dimensional spatial
                                         structures when encoding 3D tokens, and its relative dis-
                                         tance computation overlooks angular dependencies hinder-
                                         ing the model’s ability to capture directional variations                                                                                Heatmap
                                                                                                           z                     z                     z




                                         in visual representations. To overcome these limitations,
                                         we introduce Spherical Coordinate–based Positional Em-
                                         bedding (SoPE). Our method maps point-cloud token in-                     (a) RoPE              (b) RoPE-3D          (c) SoPE

                                         dices into a 3D spherical coordinate space, enabling uni-
                                                                                                           Figure 1.      SoPE enhances 3D spatial representation via
                                         fied modeling of spatial locations and directional angles.        geometry-aware positional encoding. Conventional positional
                                         This formulation preserves the inherent geometric structure       encoding methods such as (a) RoPE and (b) RoPE-3D exhibit spa-
                                         of point-cloud data, enhances spatial awareness, and yields       tial perception bias: cross-modal attention concentrates on a few
                                         more consistent and expressive geometric representations          hotspots and fails to capture global context, resulting in less dis-
                                         for multimodal learning. In addition, we introduce a multi-       criminative spatial features. In contrast, the proposed (c) SoPE
                                         scale frequency mixing strategy to fuse feature information       produces more balanced and global attention patterns while am-
                                         across different frequency domains. Experimental results          plifying spatial feature saliency, indicating a deeper understanding
                                         on multiple 3D scene benchmarks validate the effectiveness        of the 3D environment.
                                         of our approach, while real-world deployment experiments
                                         further demonstrate its strong generalization capability.
                                                                                                           tures that can interface with language, prior work has fol-
                                                                                                           lowed several routes: projecting point clouds into im-
                                                                                                           ages [13, 21, 23, 24, 57, 83], directly encoding 3D geom-

4. Method                                                             In Sec. 4.1, we extend the temporal positional index to in-
                                                                      clude four components: temporal position t, radius r, po-
We propose Spherical Coordinate–Based Positional Em-                  lar angle θ, and azimuthal angle ϕ. In this work we split
bedding (SoPE), a positional encoding variant tailored to             the frequency spectrum into four proportional parts cor-
3D point-cloud tokens. As illustrated in Figure 3, SoPE               responding to these components, with an allocation ratio
reparameterizes point-cloud tokens from Cartesian coor-               t : r : θ : ϕ = 24 : 2 : 3 : 3. To determine this design
dinates into a spherical coordinate system, enhancing the             we ran extensive ablation experiments comparing many al-
model’s sensitivity to both spatial positions and directional         ternative allocations and band-orderings; the results guided
variations. SoPE comprises three key components: spheri-              our choice of both the per-component bandwidths and the
cal coordinate positional projection, multi-dimensional fre-          subband ordering used in the final model. Concretely, we
quency allocation, and multi-scale frequency encoding.                map the three spherical-coordinate components r, θ, ϕ to
                                                                      the front higher-frequency subbands and place the tempo-
4.1. Spherical Coordinate Positional Projection                       ral component t in the later lower-frequency subbands. In-
Spherical coordinate positional projection, decouples 3D              tuitively, assigning the spherical components to higher fre-
spatial tokens from the 1D textual sequence by replac-                quencies helps the model capture fine-grained spatial and
ing the flattened raster index with a geometry-aware tuple            angular variations and directional cues, while allocating a
(t, r, θ, ϕ).This process comprises two key steps:                    larger low-frequency block to the temporal component pre-
    (i) Positional Index Reallocation: We extract the Carte-          serves slower, long-range temporal dynamics and continu-
sian coordinates (x, y, z) of point cloud tokens to repre-            ity. This allocation achieved the best trade-off between spa-
sent their intrinsic 3D spatial positions, while preserving           tial and angular resolution and temporal coherence in our
the original RoPE-assigned index t to maintain their tem-             ablation studies. The final relative rotation matrix is formu-
poral ordering within the sequence. Each token is thereby             lated as follows:

Figure 3. SoPE: Spherical Coordinate-Based Positional Embedding for Multimodal 3D Scene Understanding. The figure illustrates
the overall SpatialSoPE framework, where SoPE is integrated into SpatialLM. By transforming coordinates from Cartesian to spherical,
SpatialSoPE mitigates spatial directional bias and enables more robust 3D object understanding and localization.

5.3. Ablation Studies
Comparison of Frequency Allocation Schemes. Under
identical settings, we perform a controlled study that varies
only the frequency allocation strategy in SpatialSoPE. As
shown in Table 5, our allocation consistently outperforms
all alternatives, suggesting that overemphasizing tempo-
ral frequencies harms geometric and orientation modeling,
while overemphasizing angular/spatial frequencies under-
mines sequence-level stability. By reserving low-frequency
capacity for long-range temporal coherence and assigning               Figure 6. The figure illustrates the real-world experimental envi-
high-frequency bandwidth to spherical components, Spa-                 ronment and the physical robot used in our study. Equipped with
tialSoPE more accurately separates local from global 3D                SpatialSoPE, the robot is capable of understanding the entire scene
structure.                                                             and executing exploration and object-transport tasks according to
Comparison of Multi-scale Frequency Mixing Strategy.                   human instructions.
As shown in Table 6, we further evaluate the Multi-scale
Frequency Mixing Strategy on both SpatialLM+RoPE-                      we reconstruct and render a point cloud of the environment
3D and SpatialSoPE. For SpatialLM+RoPE-3D, although                    using MASt3R-SLAM [46]. Next, SpatialSoPE processes
(x, y, z) are encoded in Cartesian coordinates, multi-scale            the reconstructed scene to produce semantic labels, bound-
mixing brings only modest gains and mainly acts as a                   ing boxes, and other object-level information. This infor-
smoothing operation. In contrast, the same design yields               mation is then converted into a textual scene graph, from
clearly larger improvements for SpatialSoPE, where coarse              which we generate navigation target points—following a
scales preserve global layout and temporal stability, and fine         design similar to Work [20, 44, 50]—based on the bound-
scales emphasize small objects, boundaries, and orientation            ing boxes of each piece of furniture for global path plan-
differences. Built on top of spherical reparameterization              ning. Finally, inspired by Work [37, 72], we employ LLMs
and tailored frequency allocation, the multi-scale strategy            as the robot’s high-level task planner, encapsulating naviga-
allows SpatialSoPE to better disentangle local and global              tion, grasping, placing, and other behaviors into atomic ac-
3D structure, leading to more stable detection and more ac-            tions. Built upon SpatialSoPE’s scene understanding, this
curate spatial perception.                                             enables general and efficient task planning for the robot.

                                               Supplementary Material
                                                                         We further integrate the multimodal GPT-4o model to
                                                                      obtain scene understanding and action-level feedback in
                                                                      real-world environments. After each action, the manipula-
                                                                      tor’s wrist camera captures the current scene to assess exe-
                                                                      cution success and overall task progress. For example, once
                                                                      the mobile robot reaches a new piece of furniture, GPT-
Figure 7. Detection visualization and task environments of Spa-
                                                                      4o identifies the objects on it to support exploration in un-
tialSoPE in real-world reconstructed scenes.                          known environments. Similarly, after each picking or plac-
                                                                      ing operation, GPT-4o verifies whether the action was exe-
                                                                      cuted correctly. Additional feedback, such as pose estima-
7. Real-World Validation                                              tion or inverse-kinematics results, can also be incorporated
                                                                      into the evaluation process.
